title: The four churchwomen (1980)
hook: Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan, killed in El Salvador

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oscar Romero, who read the names of the dead on Sunday radio. Your line was the voice of the voiceless. Whose story did you carry? Today, four women in the same country. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

Two of them have just flown back from a meeting in Nicaragua. The other two have driven out to meet them, after dark, at the airport outside San Salvador, in a white van. Four American women: two Maryknoll sisters, an Ursuline sister and a young lay volunteer. They know the roads, the checkpoints, the risk. The van never reaches home. Days later, local people point the way to a shallow grave by a country road. Their names were Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan.
screen: `A VAN LEAVES THE AIRPORT.` → `FOUR WOMEN, ONE ROAD.` → `IT NEVER REACHES HOME.`

segments.voice: It would be easy to tell this as a story about how they died. Their lives say more. First, who they were. Maura Clarke and Ita Ford were Maryknoll sisters, members of an American Catholic missionary order. Dorothy Kazel was an Ursuline sister from Cleveland. Jean Donovan was not a nun at all. She was a lay missionary, a young woman with a business career behind her, who had come to help. Second, what they did. In a country at war, they drove refugees to safety, brought food and medicine to families hiding from the fighting, and helped bury the dead. Ordinary work, done in a place where ordinary work had become dangerous. Third, the choice to stay. Friends and family asked them to come home. Jean Donovan wrote that she had thought about leaving, but couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for. They knew what had happened to Romero. They stayed with the poor. Fourth, the truth told. Members of El Salvador's National Guard were later convicted of the killings, and questions about who gave the orders went on for years. Their families kept asking. Some Catholics read their story beside words Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have called you friends." Just before it, he says he will no longer call them servants. Not servants. Friends. These women had not gone to El Salvador to die. They had gone to be with people, and when staying became dangerous, they kept being with them.
screen: `THREE SISTERS AND A VOLUNTEER.` · `REFUGEES, FOOD, BURIALS.` · `ASKED TO LEAVE, THEY STAYED.` · `THE KILLERS CONVICTED, QUESTIONS REMAIN.` · then, large: `BUT I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold missionaries in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone far from home tonight because they chose to be with people who need help: a sister in a clinic, a volunteer at a border, a lay worker in a refugee camp, a doctor in a war zone. You don't need a name. Notice what their day might hold: a long drive, a checkpoint, a child who needs medicine. If you pray, you can pray for missionaries, and for the people they stay with. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and wish them safe roads. The bell holds the time.
Jean Donovan. The lay missionary among the four churchwomen killed in El Salvador, who wrote that she couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for.
Your line: they stayed with the poor. Today, stay a little longer with someone you'd usually hurry past. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Maryknoll, the Ursulines of Cleveland and parishes in El Salvador and the United States remember the four churchwomen with Masses and vigils, especially on the anniversary of their deaths.
